messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Car Similarity: Similar cars, Media Exposure: Related media content, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Smoking: I smoke
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Before the summer he turned twenty-three, Miguel had never thought of himself as someone who could be broken. He had grown up in a small town in Jalisco, worked cleaning houses since he was sixteen, and moved to the United States at twenty-one with a work visa and a wife who believed they would build something steady. By the time he was twenty-five, that wife was gone, and Miguel was living alone in a studio apartment in Houston, waking up three or four times every night to check that the door was locked. He would lie still in the dark, listening to the hum of the window unit, and only fall back asleep when he had confirmed, with his own hand on the deadbolt, that no one had come in.

The thing that had happened to him had happened in a parking lot behind a strip mall, on a Tuesday afternoon in late August. He had been walking back to his car after finishing a shift at a motel when a sedan pulled up beside him—a dark blue Honda, common enough that he had seen three just like it that same week. Two men got out. They were wearing uniforms, or something close to uniforms: dark polo shirts with a logo on the chest, the kind of thing that might belong to a security company or a towing service. They asked for his papers. He showed them his work permit. They said it was fake. They said they were going to call immigration. And then they did not call anyone. Instead, they drove him to a warehouse on the edge of town, and for the next six hours they asked him questions he could not answer, and when he could not answer, they used a Taser on his ribs and a plastic bottle filled with water and a rag over his face. He had wet himself. He had begged. He had told them everything he knew about everyone he knew, and still they kept going. Eventually they let him go, dumped him on a curb with his wallet empty and his phone gone, and said if he told anyone, they would find him again.

That was three years ago. Miguel had not told anyone. He had not filed a police report. He had not told his wife, who had left him six months later because he had become someone she did not recognize—someone who flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, someone who smoked cigarette after cigarette on the balcony at night, staring at the street. He had not told his boss at the cleaning service, though he had started requesting only morning shifts so he would never have to walk to his car after dark. He had not told the therapist at the free clinic, because he had only gone once and then stopped.

What brought him to the clinic now, at twenty-six, was a Tuesday much like that other Tuesday—hot, humid, the kind of sky that pressed down on you. He had been standing at a bus stop after an appointment, and a dark blue sedan had slowed as it passed him. The driver had been an older woman with gray hair, probably lost, probably looking for an address. But Miguel’s chest had seized. His vision had gone spotty. He had dropped his cigarette and walked—not run, because running would have drawn attention—into the nearest store, a dollar store, and stood in the cleaning aisle until his hands stopped shaking. That night he had smoked half a pack and checked the lock on his door seven times before he could lie down.

He was certain, in a way that felt like simple fact, that the men who had taken him were still out there, still looking for him. He did not know why they would be—he had nothing they wanted, he had told them nothing useful—but the certainty lived in his body, not his mind. When a stranger approached him on the sidewalk, even an old woman asking for directions, his pulse would spike before he could think. When someone touched him unexpectedly—a hand on his arm, a brush in a crowd—he would jerk away with a sound that embarrassed him. He had stopped going to the grocery store. He had stopped answering calls from numbers he did not recognize. He had stopped feeling anything close to safe, and he had also stopped feeling much of anything else. Positive emotions had become confusing, even frightening. A moment of laughter with a coworker would leave him disoriented, as though he had forgotten how to be in his own skin, and he would retreat to the break room and light a cigarette.

He had come to the clinic because the cleaning aisle in the dollar store had been the last straw. He had been standing there, holding a bottle of bleach, and he had thought: *I cannot live like this anymore.* He did not know if he could live any other way. What he was most afraid of, as he sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, was that the therapist would tell him the same thing the men in the warehouse had told him—that he was lying, that he was making it up, that he deserved what happened. What he was hoping for, though he could barely admit it even to himself, was that someone might finally believe him.
